title: How do you solve a growth case from start to finish, with a fully worked example?
description: The complete growth case guide: sorting and sizing every option, worked through a gym chain's 20% revenue target, plus mistakes and practice prompts.
hook: Growth cases invite you to list ideas, and that is the trap. Strong candidates sort the options, size the biggest ones and show whether they add up to the target. Here is how that looks with real numbers.
body:
In this guide

  • When you will meet this case
  • The structure, and the first question to ask
  • A fully worked example with real numbers
  • The mistakes that cost candidates this case
  • Phrases to use
  • Practice prompts with model answers

When you will meet this case

The client wants more revenue and is open to options.

The structure

How much growth, by when? Which business units grow today, and is anything off the table?
  • With our existing products
    • Sell more to current customers (more visits · bigger orders · loyalty app)
    • Reach new customers or markets (new cities · segments · channels)
  • With new products
    • For current customers (beans and pods for home · subscriptions)
    • For new customers (diversify) (bottled drinks in supermarkets)

Risk rises as you move away from what the client already sells to whom. Size each option, then say how: build it, partner or buy.

A fully worked example

The prompt: a gym chain wants to grow revenue by 20% in three years, from £50M to £60M. How?

Step 1: understand today's revenue. 100,000 members × £35 a month × 12 = £42M from memberships, plus £8M from personal training and extras.

Step 2: sort and size the options.

OptionWorkingExtra revenue
Raise the monthly fee by £2100,000 × £2 × 12£2.4M
Open 10 new gyms10 × 1,500 members × £35 × 12£6.3M
Grow personal training and extrasLift extras by about a fifth£1.5M
Total£10.2M (about 20%)

Step 3: so what. New gyms are the biggest lever but carry the most risk and upfront cost. The price rise is quick but could raise cancellations.

Recommendation: "The target is reachable with three moves, worth about £10M together: ten new gyms (£6.3M), a £2 price rise (£2.4M) and more personal training (£1.5M). I'd start with the price rise and extras, which are fast and cheap, while choosing sites for new gyms. The main risk is that the price rise increases cancellations, so I'd test it in a few locations first."

The mistakes that cost candidates this case

  1. Listing ten ideas with no sizing and no priority.
  2. Not checking whether the options actually add up to the target.
  3. Ignoring cost and risk: the biggest option is not always the best.
  4. Forgetting that more customers can mean more churn or cannibalisation.

Phrases to use

Let me size the three biggest options and check whether they reach the £10M target.
New gyms are the biggest lever, but slowest and riskiest, so I'd sequence them after the quick wins.

Practise with these prompts

Should a coffee chain sell its beans in supermarkets?

Show a model structure
  • Market: Size of premium coffee in supermarkets; Competitors and shelf space
  • Economics: Price, retailer margin, our cost; Volume needed to pay back
  • Cannibalisation and halo: Café visits lost vs new customers; Brand awareness gained
  • Brand and operations: Premium image on a shelf next to discounts; Roasting and supply capacity

Where to start: Net profit after the café visits we might lose.

The trap: Ignoring the effect on café visits and on a premium brand.

How should a newspaper grow digital subscriptions?

Show a model structure
  • Reach: Traffic: search, social, newsletters; New audiences and topics
  • Conversion: Paywall design, trials, price; Sign-up friction
  • Retention: Engagement habits, apps, bundles; Cancellation process and win-back
  • Revenue per subscriber: Tiers, family plans, add-ons; Annual vs monthly

Where to start: The funnel: find the step with the biggest drop-off.

The trap: Only listing marketing ideas without the reach → convert → retain funnel.

How can a university attract more international students?

Show a model structure
  • Markets: Which countries have demand; Competition from other countries
  • Offer: Courses, price, scholarships; Rankings and graduate jobs
  • Recruitment: Agents, partners, digital; Conversion from offer to arrival
  • Barriers: Visas and policy; Housing and support

Where to start: Conversion from offer to arrival: many offers are lost to visas and competitors.

The trap: Ignoring visas and housing, which often limit numbers.
